Thanks again for the demo this morning. We got a few finance/procurement questions that I want to make sure I captured correctly before we loop them into a formal RFP:

1) When you say "tokens" in the pricing sheet, is that the same as characters? Our engineering team reports usage today in characters and it's not obvious how to translate.
2) How do cached prompts affect billing? If we cache a 500-char prompt and only send a 50-char user message, are we billed for the 550 chars (or tokens) or just the 50?
3) Are there any per-request charges (e.g., per HTTP call) on top of token billing, or is everything per-token?
4) For budgeting purposes our finance lead asked for a target unit e.g. $/1M tokens — can you give a ballpark number for the model you demoed (redwood-llama-v2-13b-quant)?

Attached is the LumenPay-usage-sample.csv that maps a couple of our common request types (onboarding flow, balance lookup, message generation) in characters. If you can return a short mapping + an illustrative cost table it will help us decide whether to move to a sandbox trial.

Thanks for the clear summary, Alice — good questions. Short answer first, then a few worked examples using your sample: 

Summary answers:
- "Tokens" are NOT the same as characters; tokens are model-tokenizer units. A rough conversion is ~4 characters per token for English (so 1M tokens ≈ 4M chars) but it varies by language and punctuation.
- Billing is based on billed tokens processed by the runtime (prompt + completion). If a cached prefix is served entirely from our prefix cache and does not need to be re-tokenized/processed, you will not be billed for it. In practice caching reduces billed tokens but does not change the API-level request count.
- There is no separate per-request billing line item for hosted inference in the plan we discussed — billing is per-token. Rate limits/requests-per-second exist for throttling but don't add to cost.
- Ballpark: for the redwood-llama-v2-13b-quant model, effective cost to you on the hosted plan (post-volume discounts and typical batching) is roughly $30–$60 per 1M billed tokens depending on caching and batching. I can run the exact math against your CSV.

Worked example from your sample (high level):
- Onboarding prompt: 2,400 characters (≈600 tokens) + model response 1,000 chars (≈250 tokens) => ~850 billed tokens if prompt was not cached. If we cache a 1,800-char static prefix (≈450 tokens) and serve from cache, billed tokens drop to ~400.

Next steps I propose:
1) I'll attach a quick "pricing cheatsheet" that shows tokens↔chars conversion ranges and sample $/1M tokens math.
2) If it's useful, we can run a one-week sandbox where you push real requests into a dedicated test key; we'll return a detailed projection for a 30/90/365 day burn with low/median/high cache hit assumptions.
3) 30-minute follow-up call — can we do Monday 10am PT?

I'll also let Monica add the deeper technical notes on cache behavior for your infra team.

Thanks,

Hi Alice — a couple technical clarifications to Karthik's note so your engineering/procurement folks have the right expectations: 

1) What we mean by "cached prompt" — we support two common caching layers: prefix cache (server-side KV of encoded tokens) and client-side cached artifacts (you can store and re-send a message id). A prefix cache hit means the runtime can reuse the KV cache and avoid re-computing attention over the prefix; in that case billed tokens are only the new tokens that require computation (usually the user message + generation). If the prefix is large and fully matched, the billed token count can be dramatically lower.

2) Edge cases to watch: if you vary the prefix slightly (e.g., include a timestamp or session id inside the prefix) the cache will miss and you will be billed for the whole sequence (prefix+new). Best practice: keep static instructional text separate from per-user variables so we can cache the static portion.

3) Request vs token visibility: we surface both metrics in the Redwood Console. Billing is token-based, but your engineering dashboards may still want request counts for latency/rate planning.

4) Practical numbers we see in similar customers: 40–70% cache hit on templated onboarding flows reduces billed tokens by ~35–60% overall. Batching across concurrent requests also lowers the effective cost because quoting/overhead per request is amortized.

If useful I can produce a short CSV that maps your provided character counts to token estimates under conservative/median/optimistic assumptions — happy to produce that ahead of the call.

Monica Patel
Senior Solutions Engineer, Redwood Inference
